summary: Defines metrics for measuring connectivity between a pair of Internet hosts. It replaced RFC 2498.

plainLanguage.summary: Before you can measure how fast a network is, you need a way to say whether two computers can reach each other at all. This RFC defines that way: a set of named measurements, each with the hosts, the time and the length of the interval it applies to, and a yes-or-no answer.

questions: how many probe packets for connectivity test
subtitle: Named measurements for whether two hosts can reach each other, and how to take them.

tldr.problem: Connectivity is the base of the Internet, so any measurement suite needs a precise way to say whether a pair of hosts can reach each other. Vague wording makes results from different tools impossible to compare.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a family of metrics, each with a name, parameters, units and a definition. They build from one-way and two-way connectivity at a single instant to connectivity across an interval, ending with Type-P1-P2-Interval-Temporal-Connectivity and a method for estimating it.
tldr.outcome: A measurement can now be reported in terms everyone agrees on, with recommended values for the interval, the waiting time and the number of probes. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2498 and warns that probing can be abused.

today: RFC 2678 is a Proposed Standard published in September 1999. It obsoletes RFC 2498, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Connectivity as a Set of Named Metrics
sections.content:
Connectivity is the basic stuff from which the Internet is made, so metrics determining whether pairs of hosts, identified by IP addresses, can reach each other must form the base of a measurement suite. The RFC defines several such metrics, some of which serve mainly as building blocks for the others. It builds on the notions introduced in RFC 2330, the IPPM framework document, and the reader is assumed to be familiar with that document.

The RFC sets out the structure of the memo. An analytic metric, called Type-P-Instantaneous-Unidirectional-Connectivity, defines one-way connectivity at one moment in time. Using that metric, a second analytic metric, Type-P-Instantaneous-Bidirectional-Connectivity, defines two-way connectivity at one moment in time. Using these, the corresponding one-way and two-way analytic metrics are defined for connectivity over an interval of time. Using these again, an analytic metric called Type-P1-P2-Interval-Temporal-Connectivity defines a useful notion of two-way connectivity between two hosts over an interval of time. Methodologies are then presented for estimating it in a variety of settings.

The RFC names the careful definition of Type-P1-P2-Interval-Temporal-Connectivity, together with the discussion of the metric and the methodologies for estimating it, as the two chief contributions of the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you can measure how fast a network is, you need a way to say whether two computers can reach each other at all. This RFC defines that way: a set of named measurements, each with the hosts, the time and the length of the interval it applies to, and a yes-or-no answer.

sections.title: Instantaneous One-Way Connectivity
sections.content:
The first metric is Type-P-Instantaneous-Unidirectional-Connectivity. Its parameters are Src, the IP address of a host, Dst, the IP address of a host, and T, a time. Its units are Boolean.

The definition is short. Src has Type-P-Instantaneous-Unidirectional-Connectivity to Dst at time T if a type-P packet transmitted from Src to Dst at time T will arrive at Dst. The letter P stands for the type of packet, so the same question can be asked of a TCP segment, a UDP datagram or an ICMP echo.

The RFC notes that for most applications, such as any TCP connection, bidirectional connectivity is considerably more germane than unidirectional connectivity, although unidirectional connectivity can be of interest for some security applications, for example testing whether a firewall correctly filters out a ping of death. Most applications also require connectivity over an interval, while this metric is instantaneous, though again instantaneous connectivity remains of interest for some security applications. One might not have instantaneous connectivity because of a transient event such as a full queue at a router, even if at nearby instants one does have connectivity.

The RFC also points out that it has not explicitly defined when the packet arrives at Dst. The TTL field in IP packets is meant to limit packet lifetimes to 255 seconds (RFC 791). In practice the TTL field can be strictly a hop count (RFC 1812), with most Internet hops being much shorter than one second, so most packets will have nowhere near the 255 second lifetime. In principle, however, packets might survive longer than 255 seconds, so consideration of packet lifetimes must be taken into account when attempting to measure the value of this metric.

Finally, the RFC observes that one might assume unidirectional connectivity is hard to measure without connectivity in the reverse direction. A process on Dst's host could instead note when it receives packets from Src and report the fact over an external channel, or later when Dst does have connectivity to Src. Such a methodology could reliably measure the unidirectional connectivity this metric defines.
sections.plainLanguage: The simplest measurement asks whether a packet sent from one address at one moment would reach the other address. The answer is yes or no. The RFC notes that a packet's lifetime matters here, because the TTL field in an IP packet is meant to limit its life to 255 seconds.

sections.title: Instantaneous Two-Way Connectivity
sections.content:
The second metric is Type-P-Instantaneous-Bidirectional-Connectivity. Its parameters are A1, the IP address of a host, A2, the IP address of a host, and T, a time. Its units are Boolean.

Addresses A1 and A2 have Type-P-Instantaneous-Bidirectional-Connectivity at time T if address A1 has Type-P-Instantaneous-Unidirectional-Connectivity to address A2 and address A2 has Type-P-Instantaneous-Unidirectional-Connectivity to address A1.

The RFC then gives an alternative definition. A1 and A2 are fully connected if at time T address A1 has instantaneous connectivity to address A2, and at time T+dT address A2 has instantaneous connectivity to A1, where T+dT is when the packet sent from A1 arrives at A2. The RFC says this definition is more useful for measurement, because the measurement can use a reply from A2 to A1 in order to assess full connectivity. It is a more complex definition, however, because it breaks the symmetry between A1 and A2, and requires a notion of quantifying how long a particular packet from A1 takes to reach A2. The RFC postpones that distinction until the interval-connectivity metrics.
sections.plainLanguage: Two-way connectivity at one moment means both directions work at that same moment. The RFC points out an easier alternative: a packet from the first host arrives at the second at a slightly later time, and the second replies at that moment. That is easier to measure, because the reply is the evidence, but it breaks the symmetry between the two hosts.

sections.title: Connectivity Over an Interval
sections.content:
Section 4 of the RFC defines Type-P-Interval-Unidirectional-Connectivity. Its parameters are Src, Dst, T, a time, and dT, a duration, so that the closed interval [T, T+dT] denotes a time interval. Its units are Boolean.

Address Src has Type-P-Interval-Unidirectional-Connectivity to address Dst during the interval [T, T+dT] if for some T' within [T, T+dT] it has Type-P-Instantaneous-Unidirectional-Connectivity to Dst.

Section 5 defines Type-P-Interval-Bidirectional-Connectivity with the same kind of parameters: A1 and A2, the IP addresses of two hosts, T, and dT, again denoting the closed interval [T, T+dT]. Its units are Boolean as well. Addresses A1 and A2 have Type-P-Interval-Bidirectional-Connectivity between them during the interval if address A1 has Type-P-Interval-Unidirectional-Connectivity to address A2 during the interval and address A2 has Type-P-Interval-Unidirectional-Connectivity to address A1 during the interval.

The RFC is explicit that this metric is not quite what is needed for defining generally useful connectivity. That requires the notion that a packet sent from A1 to A2 can elicit a response from A2 that will reach A1. With this definition, it could be that A1 and A2 have full connectivity but only at a time early enough in the interval that neither can reply to packets sent by the other. The RFC says this deficiency motivates the next metric.
sections.plainLanguage: The next two measurements cover a period rather than a moment. One-way connectivity over an interval holds if there is at least one moment inside the interval when the packet would arrive. Two-way connectivity over an interval holds if each host has a working moment toward the other somewhere inside the interval. The RFC notes a gap: the two working moments might not overlap, so neither host could actually answer the other's packet.

sections.title: Two-Way Temporal Connectivity and How to Measure It
sections.content:
The final metric is Type-P1-P2-Interval-Temporal-Connectivity, with parameters Src, Dst, T and dT, and Boolean units. The RFC defines it as follows. Address Src has Type-P1-P2-Interval-Temporal-Connectivity to address Dst during the interval [T, T+dT] if there exist times T1 and T2, and intervals dT1 and dT2, such that:

  • T1, T1+dT1, T2 and T2+dT2 are all in [T, T+dT].
  • T1+dT1 is less than or equal to T2.
  • At time T1, Src has Type-P1 instantaneous connectivity to Dst.
  • At time T2, Dst has Type-P2 instantaneous connectivity to Src.
  • dT1 is the time taken for a Type-P1 packet sent by Src at time T1 to arrive at Dst.
  • dT2 is the time taken for a Type-P2 packet sent by Dst at time T2 to arrive at Src.

The RFC says this metric defines generally useful connectivity: Src can send a packet to Dst that elicits a response. Because many applications use different types of packets for forward and reverse traffic, the metric allows different packet types in the two directions.

Section 6.6 sketches a class of methodologies for estimating the metric. It is a class rather than a single methodology because the particulars depend on the types P1 and P2. The inputs are the types P1 and P2, the addresses A1 and A2, the interval [T, T+dT], N, the number of packets to send as probes, and W, the waiting time, which bounds for how long it is useful to wait for a reply to a packet. The RFC requires that W be at most 255 and that dT be greater than W, and it recommends dT of 60 seconds, W of 10 seconds and N of 20 packets.

The algorithm is: compute N sending times randomly and uniformly distributed over [T, T+dT-W]; at each sending time, transmit from A1 a well-formed packet of type P1 to A2; inspect incoming network traffic to A1 to determine if a successful reply is received, and if any successful reply is received the value of the measurement is true, which ends the measurement; if no successful replies are received by time T+dT, the value is false.

The RFC notes that the algorithm is inexact, because it does not and cannot probe temporal connectivity at every instant between T and T+dT. The value of N trades measurement precision against network measurement load, and the RFC says the state of the art in Internet research does not yet offer solid guidance for picking N, so the values given are guidelines.

For TCP, the RFC gives a specific methodology. A TCP-port-N1-port-N2 methodology sends TCP SYN packets with source port N1 and destination port N2 at address A2. Incoming traffic to A1 is then interpreted: a SYN-ack from A2 with the proper acknowledgement fields and ports indicates temporal connectivity, and the measurement terminates immediately with the value true. A RST packet from A2 with the proper ports indicates temporal connectivity between the addresses, and a lack of service connectivity for that port pair. An ICMP port-unreachable from A2 indicates temporal connectivity between the addresses, and again a lack of service connectivity. An ICMP host-unreachable or network-unreachable to A1, not necessarily from A2, with an enclosed IP header matching what was sent from A1 to A2, suggests a lack of temporal connectivity; if by time T+dT no evidence of temporal connectivity has been gathered, its receipt can be used as additional information for the value false. The RFC adds that similar methodologies are needed for ICMP Echo, UDP and others.
sections.plainLanguage: The last measurement fixes that gap. It holds when a packet sent from the first host at some time inside the interval arrives at the second host, and a reply sent back at a later time inside the same interval reaches the first host. The two packet types may differ. The RFC then gives a measurement method: send a number of probes at random times inside the interval, and stop as soon as a reply arrives.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC refers back to RFC 2330, which notes that active measurement techniques, such as those defined in this document, can be abused for denial-of-service attacks disguised as legitimate measurement activity.

It adds that testing for connectivity can be used to probe firewalls and other security mechanisms for weak spots.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC warns that sending probes can be abused for denial-of-service attacks disguised as measurement, and that testing connectivity can be used to look for weak spots in firewalls and other security mechanisms.

viz.caption: THE FIVE METRICS DEFINED BY RFC 2678

items.title: Instantaneous one-way
items.text: Would a packet sent from Src to Dst at time T arrive?

items.title: Instantaneous two-way
items.text: Does that hold in both directions at the same time?

items.title: Interval one-way
items.text: Does that hold at some moment inside [T, T+dT]?

items.title: Interval two-way
items.text: Does each host have such a moment toward the other?

items.title: Interval temporal
items.text: Can a packet get through and the reply get back, both inside the interval?
